label: HiFi Jazz
rationale: Harold Land's finest record and the best argument for him as an underrated composer: a 1959 Los Angeles quintet date on the short-lived HiFi Jazz label (Contemporary picked it up in 1969, OJC in 1991) with Elmo Hope contributing four of the six tunes and Dupree Bolton — the brilliant, almost unrecorded trumpeter — alongside him. The Penguin Guide to Jazz calls Land 'an underrated composer with a deep feeling for the blues' and says the album, 'tricky and fugitive as much of it is, must be thought his finest moment'; DownBeat gave it 4.5 stars on release (Ralph J. Gleason, May 1960), AllMusic 4.5 (Scott Yanow: 'high-quality hard bop'), Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide 4/5. Lineage and session gravity both point the same way for this canon: Land is the West Coast hard-bop voice that connects the Clifford Brown-Max Roach band to the Curtis Counce group and the Harold Land-Bobby Hutcherson partnership, Elmo Hope is a canonical hard-bop pianist the collection does not yet hold, and Dupree Bolton appears on almost nothing else — Ted Gioia wrote a feature-length search for him. The canon has no Harold Land album and only one Elmo Hope-adjacent record, so this fills a real hole in the West Coast wing rather than duplicating a name.
scope_flag: Squarely inside the window (1959-60) and inside hard bop; no boundary call. The only question for the council is priority — the album's reputation rests on the Penguin/DownBeat line ('his finest moment') rather than on repeated canon-list appearances, which is consensus of a thinner kind.

ballot.case_for: The strongest case is a defining statement with exceptional session gravity: the Penguin Guide calls it Land’s “finest moment,” while the dossier reports 4.5-star assessments from DownBeat and AllMusic, supporting substantial critical esteem across contemporary and retrospective criticism (S1; S2). Elmo Hope composed four of the six selections, and the documented quintet of Land, Hope, Dupree Bolton, Herbie Lewis, and Frank Butler makes this a distinctive collaborative statement rather than a routine hard-bop date (S1, S3). Land’s connections to the Brown–Roach, Curtis Counce, and later Bobby Hutcherson ensembles give it a persuasive, though partly inferential, lineage case; its concentrated encounter with Hope and the sparsely recorded Bolton offers particular discovery value.
ballot.case_against: The dossier establishes critical acclaim more securely than the rubric’s strongest signal: repeated appearances in independent canon lists or documented musician testimony. Much of the Penguin, DownBeat, and Rolling Stone evidence is relayed through Wikipedia rather than directly preserved, and no Penguin core-collection designation or demonstrable downstream influence is established. Hope’s four compositions also qualify the rationale’s emphasis on Land as an underrated composer: this may be Land’s defining recording without being chiefly his compositional statement.
ballot.disagreement: The references agree on contested/strong and find no scope boundary. They differ on evidentiary certainty: Reference 2 treats Land’s artistic-peak status and Bolton’s extremely limited recording output as settled, while Reference 1 qualifies the defining-statement claim and challenges the breadth of the Bolton scarcity claim; the defensible shared ground is a rare featured Bolton appearance, not a near-complete account of his discography.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John give The Fox strong listening consideration as a potential defining Land record, while weighing its specialist critical stature against the thinner evidence of broad canonical consensus.
